title: Pathogens and diseases
notes: Pathogens are disease-causing microorganisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, helminths.
- **Cholera**: Vibrio cholerae, waterborne, causes severe diarrhea
- **Typhoid**: Salmonella typhi, fecal-oral, fever, abdominal pain
- **Hepatitis B**: Hepatitis B virus, blood/body fluids, liver
- **HIV/AIDS**: Human Immunodeficiency Virus, destroys CD4+ T cells
- **Rabies**: Rabies virus, animal bite, affects nervous system
- **Malaria**: Plasmodium (P. falciparum, P. vivax), Anopheles mosquito

summary: Pathogens are disease-causing organisms — bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths — and each group produces a characteristic pattern of illness. Bacterial diseases include tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, diphtheria and pertussis; viral diseases include influenza, dengue, hepatitis B, HIV/AIDS and rabies; protozoan diseases such as malaria and amoebiasis are usually food-borne or vector-borne, and helminthic diseases such as ascariasis and filariasis involve parasitic worms. Antibiotics act only on bacteria because viruses have none of the bacterial structures that these drugs target. Prevention relies on sanitation, safe drinking water, vector control, personal hygiene and vaccination.
importantConcepts: Pathogens are the disease-causing microorganisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths (worms).
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no independent metabolism; they can multiply only inside a living host cell, which is why antibiotics do not act on them.
Vectors carry pathogens from one host to another: Aedes aegypti for dengue and chikungunya, Anopheles for malaria, the tsetse fly for sleeping sickness and the sandfly for kala-azar.

Routes of transmission include airborne (tuberculosis, influenza, diphtheria), waterborne and faecal-oral (cholera, typhoid, amoebiasis), vector-borne (malaria, dengue, filariasis) and contact through blood or body fluids (hepatitis B, HIV).

Antibiotics act on bacterial structures and processes such as the peptidoglycan cell wall, the bacterial ribosome and bacterial DNA, so they have no target in a virus; their misuse also selects antibiotic-resistant strains.
Fungal pathogens such as Trichophyton and Microsporum infect the keratinised epidermis and cause superficial diseases such as ringworm and athlete's foot.
importantStatements: Antibiotics have no effect on viral infections because viruses lack a peptidoglycan cell wall and bacterial ribosomes, which are the antibiotic targets.
Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and not by a worm; the worm-borne diseases in this list are ascariasis, filariasis, taeniasis and hookworm.
Only particular mosquito species transmit disease: Aedes for dengue and chikungunya, Anopheles for malaria.
Tuberculosis and diphtheria attack the respiratory system, while cholera causes profuse watery diarrhoea with severe dehydration.
HIV attacks CD4+ helper T lymphocytes, progressively weakening cell-mediated immunity and leading to AIDS.
Rabies is a viral disease of the central nervous system spread through the saliva of a biting animal and is almost always fatal once symptoms appear.

keyPoints: Bacterial causes: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB), Vibrio cholerae (cholera), Salmonella typhi (typhoid), Corynebacterium diphtheriae (diphtheria), Bordetella pertussis (whooping cough).
Viral causes: influenza virus, rhinovirus (common cold), dengue virus, hepatitis B virus, HIV and rabies virus.
Protozoan causes: Plasmodium (malaria), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebiasis), Trypanosoma (sleeping sickness), Leishmania donovani (kala-azar).
Helminthic causes: Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Wuchereria bancrofti (filariasis or elephantiasis), Taenia solium (tapeworm from undercooked pork), Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm).
Fungal causes: Trichophyton and Microsporum cause ringworm, and dermatophytes cause athlete's foot.
Fungal infections need antifungals rather than antibiotics, and viral diseases are managed by prevention, supportive care and, where available, antivirals.
specialNotes: Antibiotics are effective only against bacteria; using them for a viral infection not only fails but also promotes antibiotic resistance in the resident flora.
Cholera and typhoid are waterborne and are prevented by safe drinking water and sanitation, whereas tuberculosis and influenza spread through the air.
Malaria is a protozoan disease and is often wrongly grouped with the worm diseases; Plasmodium is a unicellular protozoan, not a worm.
Dengue is caused by the dengue virus and not by the mosquito itself — the mosquito is only the vector, and it is the female that takes a blood meal.
Hepatitis B and HIV are transmitted through blood and body fluids, not by ordinary casual contact, whereas tuberculosis spreads by airborne droplets.
examShortTricks: Pairing anchor: TB–Mycobacterium, cholera–Vibrio, typhoid–Salmonella, malaria–Plasmodium, amoebiasis–Entamoeba.
Vector code: Aedes for dengue and chikungunya, Anopheles for malaria, sandfly for kala-azar, tsetse fly for sleeping sickness.
A worm name in the list (Ascaris, Wuchereria, Taenia, Ancylostoma) tells you immediately it is a helminthic disease.
Treatment test: if the drug given in the question is an antibiotic, the pathogen must be a bacterium.
'Bacteria and antibiotics, virus and no drug' — viruses have no cell wall for penicillin and no bacterial ribosome.
examNotes: One-mark MCQs are most often 'which organism causes this disease' or 'which is the vector of this disease', so the standard pairings must be learned.
A 5-mark table question on any four diseases with pathogen, vector, symptoms and prevention is a recurring pattern.
Antibiotic-versus-virus reasoning questions (2-3 marks) test the idea that viruses have no independent metabolism and can multiply only inside host cells.
Classifying routes of transmission as airborne, waterborne, vector-borne or contact is frequently set as a matching question worth 4-5 marks.
A diagram of the Plasmodium life cycle (sporozoite, liver stage, merozoite, gametocyte in the mosquito) appears in 4-5 mark questions.

mcs.question: Which of the following diseases is caused by a bacterium?
mcs.explanation: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis; dengue is viral, malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, and ringworm is a fungal infection.

mcs.question: Dengue fever is transmitted by the bite of:
mcs.explanation: Aedes aegypti is the vector of dengue and chikungunya. Anopheles transmits malaria, the tsetse fly transmits sleeping sickness and the sandfly transmits kala-azar.

mcs.question: Antibiotics are ineffective against influenza because:
options: The influenza virus is too large to absorb them
Viruses lack a peptidoglycan cell wall and bacterial ribosomes, which are the antibiotic targets
Antibiotics are destroyed by stomach acid before reaching the lung
Influenza is caused by a fungus
mcs.explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as the cell wall and the 70S ribosome. The influenza virus has neither and can multiply only inside host cells, so prevention, supportive care and antivirals are used instead.

mcs.question: Which disease is caused by a parasitic helminth (worm)?
mcs.explanation: Ascaris lumbricoides is a roundworm, that is a helminth. Malaria is caused by the unicellular protozoan Plasmodium, while cholera is bacterial and dengue is viral.

mcs.question: HIV/AIDS is characterised by the destruction of:
mcs.explanation: HIV infects CD4+ helper T cells, depleting them and gradually destroying cell-mediated immunity, which allows opportunistic infections to develop.
